name: StartFast
tagline: A paid Next.js starter kit that ships auth, Stripe billing, transactional email, Prisma and SEO defaults pre-wired.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: A boilerplate is the one product category where coding agents are at full strength: the deliverable is literally a folder of conventional code with no server, no network and no data behind it. An agent that knows the Next.js App Router can scaffold Prisma models, Auth.js with Google and email login, a Stripe checkout route with a webhook handler, Resend templates and sitemap plus metadata in a single session. The hard parts are not code, they are account chores: creating the Stripe product, pasting keys, verifying a sending domain, setting OAuth redirect URIs. What you pay for here is someone having already made those decisions and tested the unhappy paths, which is worth real money if your time is expensive and nearly nothing if you enjoy this part. Verify the webhook handling yourself either way, because that is where generated billing code is most often subtly wrong.
coreLoopDIY: Generates a running Next.js app with email and Google login, Prisma-backed users, a Stripe subscription checkout plus webhook that flips an entitlement flag, transactional emails and sane SEO defaults.
requirements: Stripe test-mode account and API keys for billing and webhook flows
Resend or similar SMTP provider plus a verified domain for real email delivery
Google Cloud OAuth client if you want social login
Postgres for production; SQLite is fine locally
whatYouLose: Someone else's battle-tested edge cases in Stripe webhooks: proration, failed payments, plan changes, idempotency
Ongoing updates when Next.js, Auth.js or the Stripe API moves under you
Pre-built marketing pages, pricing tables, dashboard shells and admin screens that look deliberate rather than generated
Docs and a support channel when the OAuth callback breaks at 2am
The small comfort that hundreds of other people already shipped on the same code
moatNotes: The moat is maintenance and trust, not technology. You are buying a decision log and a promise to keep it current.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a hundred dollars once is cheaper than a day of your own billable time, and because the failure modes in billing code are expensive and quiet. Boilerplate buyers are usually not short of ability, they are short of patience for the fourteenth time wiring a Stripe webhook to a user row. A maintained starter also means someone else eats the next breaking framework upgrade. The counter-argument is just as honest: generated starters get stale the moment you touch them, and plenty of people pay for a kit, rip out half of it, and end up maintaining their own fork anyway.
notes: Boilerplate is the softest target on this whole directory: the product is code and nothing else. Pay for it if you would rather skip the plumbing, not because it cannot be generated.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted SaaS starter in this empty folder. One stack, no options.

Stack: Next.js (App Router, TypeScript), Tailwind, Prisma, SQLite for local dev with a Postgres-ready schema, Auth.js v5, Stripe, Resend for email.

In scope:
1. Marketing home page, a pricing page with Free and Pro, and a privacy and terms stub. Plain, readable, no hero animations.
2. Auth.js with two providers: magic-link email via Resend, and Google OAuth. Prisma adapter, sessions in the database.
3. Prisma schema: User, Account, Session, VerificationToken, plus Subscription (userId, stripeCustomerId, stripeSubscriptionId, status, priceId, currentPeriodEnd).
4. A /dashboard route protected by middleware. Show the signed-in user, their plan, and a Pro-only panel gated by a single isPro helper derived from Subscription status.
5. Stripe: a checkout route that creates a Customer if missing and returns a Checkout Session for one recurring price from env. A billing portal route. A webhook at /api/stripe/webhook that verifies the signature with the raw body and handles checkout.session.completed, customer.subscription.updated and customer.subscription.deleted. Make webhook handling idempotent by recording processed event ids.
6. Transactional emails via Resend: login link, welcome, subscription activated. Plain React email components, no template engine.
7. SEO: per-route metadata, opengraph-image using next/og, robots.ts, sitemap.ts, JSON-LD on the home page.
8. Vitest tests for the isPro helper and the webhook handler using fixture event payloads.

Out of scope: admin panel, teams and org membership, usage metering, i18n, analytics, feature flags, any telemetry.

Rules: all secrets in .env with a committed .env.example (AUTH_SECRET, GOOGLE_ID, GOOGLE_SECRET, RESEND_API_KEY, STRIPE_SECRET_KEY, STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET, STRIPE_PRICE_ID, DATABASE_URL). No secrets in client components. No paid service calls at build time.

Finish with a README covering: npm install, prisma migrate dev, how to get each key, and how to test the webhook with the Stripe CLI including the exact listen command. Then print a short list of anything you stubbed or guessed.
